lessonTitle: Cardiac Action Potentials and Pacemaker Activity

blocks.text: A 58-year-old with advanced kidney disease misses two dialysis sessions and feels weak, with a slow, irregular pulse. His blood potassium is high. Potassium is the ion that sets the resting voltage of every heart cell, so a change of a few millimoles per litre outside the cells can slow conduction through the heart and, if severe, stop it. To see why, we need the ion currents that build the cardiac action potential.

blocks.markdown:
Heart muscle cells are excitable: when the membrane potential (the voltage inside the cell relative to outside, in mV) reaches a threshold, voltage-gated ion channels open in sequence and produce an action potential, which triggers contraction. The shape of the action potential depends on the cell type. **Ventricular myocytes** have a stable negative resting potential and an action potential with a long plateau. **Sinoatrial (SA) node cells** have no stable resting potential: they depolarise spontaneously and so set the heart rate.

Two principles help throughout. First, the membrane potential moves towards the equilibrium potential of whichever ion the membrane is most permeable to. Second, voltage-gated channels have open, closed and inactivated states; an inactivated sodium channel cannot reopen until the membrane has repolarised, which is the basis of the refractory period.

blocks.title: Resting potential, threshold and the Nernst potential
blocks.text: The resting membrane potential of a ventricular myocyte is about -90 mV, and its threshold is roughly -65 to -70 mV, so only about 20 to 25 mV of depolarisation is needed to fire it. The equilibrium (Nernst) potential of an ion is the membrane voltage at which its concentration gradient is exactly balanced by the electrical gradient. Threshold is the membrane potential at which enough voltage-gated channels open to produce a regenerative action potential. Refractory period is the time after an action potential during which a second one cannot be triggered (absolute) or needs a larger stimulus (relative).

blocks.caption: Nernst potential for potassium at 37 degrees C. [K+]o and [K+]i are extracellular and intracellular potassium concentrations in mmol/L (typical values about 4 and 140 mmol/L).

blocks.title: Why the resting potential is near EK
blocks.prompt: Calculate EK for [K+]o = 4 mmol/L and [K+]i = 140 mmol/L, and explain why the resting potential of the ventricular myocyte is close to it.

steps.text: Multiply by 61.5 mV: EK = 61.5 x (-1.544) = -95 mV.

At rest the ventricular membrane is much more permeable to K+ than to any other ion because of the open inward rectifier K+ channels (IK1), so its potential sits close to EK, at about -90 mV (slightly less negative because of small Na+ leak currents).

blocks.answer: EK is about -95 mV; the resting potential of about -90 mV lies near it because resting membrane permeability is dominated by K+.

blocks.caption: Phases of the ventricular myocyte action potential.
rows: K+ efflux through inward rectifier channels (IK1) holds the potential near EK
Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels open; large inward Na+ current
Na+ channels inactivate; brief outward K+ current (transient outward, Ito)
Inward Ca2+ through L-type channels balanced by outward K+ (delayed rectifier)
Roughly 0 mV, lasting about 200 ms (total action potential about 250 to 300 ms)
Ca2+ channels close; outward delayed-rectifier K+ current dominates

blocks.markdown: **Why the plateau matters.** The plateau keeps the membrane depolarised for about 200 ms (the whole ventricular action potential lasts about 250 to 300 ms), so Ca2+ entering through L-type channels triggers further Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum for contraction. It also makes the refractory period last almost as long as the contraction itself, so the ventricle cannot be re-excited until it has relaxed and refilled. This prevents the sustained contraction (tetanus) that would stop the heart pumping.

**Pacemaker activity in the SA node.** SA node cells have a maximum diastolic potential of about -60 mV and no stable resting level. In phase 4 they depolarise slowly and spontaneously, creating the pacemaker potential. Three components contribute. The first is the **funny current (If)**: HCN channels (hyperpolarisation-activated, cyclic-nucleotide-gated) open as the membrane repolarises and carry a slow inward current, mostly Na+. The second is a gradual decline of outward K+ current as delayed-rectifier K+ channels deactivate. The third is inward Ca2+ through T-type channels late in phase 4. When threshold (about -40 mV) is reached, L-type Ca2+ channels open and produce the upstroke (phase 0). Nodal cells have few fast Na+ channels, so the SA node upstroke is slower than in the ventricle and carried by Ca2+. Repolarisation (phase 3) is by K+ efflux. Because the SA node depolarises fastest of all cardiac cells, it sets the rhythm and is called the pacemaker.

blocks.title: Predicting the effect of a higher extracellular potassium
blocks.prompt: In hyperkalaemia [K+]o rises from 4 to 7 mmol/L, with [K+]i unchanged at 140 mmol/L. Calculate the new EK and state what happens to the resting potential and excitability.

steps.text: EK = 61.5 x (-1.301) = -80 mV, which is 15 mV less negative than -95 mV.
The resting potential follows EK, so the cell is partially depolarised (for example from -90 to about -78 mV).

Initially the cell is nearer threshold, so excitability rises slightly. If depolarisation is sustained, fast Na+ channels are held in the inactivated state and fewer can open, so the upstroke slows, conduction slows and excitability falls.

blocks.answer: EK shifts to about -80 mV. Resting potential becomes less negative; mild rises increase excitability transiently, but sustained depolarisation inactivates Na+ channels and reduces excitability and conduction.

items: Mild hyperkalaemia: resting potential is depolarised, the membrane is closer to threshold, excitability may be transiently increased.
Moderate to severe hyperkalaemia: persistent depolarisation inactivates fast Na+ channels, reducing upstroke velocity, slowing conduction and reducing excitability.
Higher extracellular K+ also increases K+ conductance, accelerating repolarisation and shortening the action potential.
Clinical consequence: conduction block and fatal arrhythmias (ventricular fibrillation or asystole).
Sodium channel inactivation, not a change in the sodium gradient, is the reason excitability falls.

blocks.title: Two cell types, two upstrokes
blocks.text: The ventricular upstroke is carried by fast Na+ channels and the plateau by L-type Ca2+ channels. The SA node upstroke is carried by L-type Ca2+ channels, and its pacemaker potential is built from the funny current, falling K+ current and T-type Ca2+ current. Remember that hyperkalaemia acts mainly by depolarising the resting potential and inactivating Na+ channels.

blocks.title: Do not assume hyperkalaemia makes cells easier to excite
blocks.text: A less negative resting potential seems closer to threshold, but sustained depolarisation inactivates the sodium channels that generate the upstroke. The net effect of significant hyperkalaemia is reduced excitability and slowed conduction.

points: The ventricular action potential has five phases: 4 (rest, IK1), 0 (fast Na+ inflow), 1 (Ito), 2 (plateau, Ca2+ in and K+ out) and 3 (K+ outflow).
The long plateau gives a long refractory period that prevents tetanus.
SA node pacemaker cells depolarise spontaneously in phase 4 via the funny current, declining K+ efflux and T-type Ca2+ current; the upstroke is carried by L-type Ca2+ channels.
Hyperkalaemia depolarises the resting potential (EK becomes less negative), then inactivates Na+ channels, slowing conduction and risking arrhythmia.

questions.stem: Which ion movement is mainly responsible for the rapid depolarisation (phase 0) of a ventricular myocyte?

options.text: Influx of Na+ through fast voltage-gated channels
Influx of Ca2+ through T-type channels
Efflux of K+ through inward rectifier channels
Efflux of Cl- through chloride channels

questions.correctOptionText: Influx of Na+ through fast voltage-gated channels

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fast Na+ channels open at threshold, producing the rapid upstroke.
distractorRationale.b: T-type Ca2+ channels contribute to nodal pacemaker activity, not ventricular phase 0.
distractorRationale.c: K+ efflux repolarises or maintains the resting potential; it does not depolarise.
distractorRationale.d: Chloride movement is not the main determinant of phase 0 in cardiac myocytes.

questions.explanation: At threshold, fast voltage-gated Na+ channels open and produce a large inward current that drives the membrane to positive values. These channels inactivate within milliseconds, which ends phase 0 and leads into phase 1.

questions.stem: What produces the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential?

options.text: Inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels balanced by outward K+ current
Continued inward Na+ current through fast channels
Outward Ca2+ current balanced by inward K+ current

questions.correctOptionText: Inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels balanced by outward K+ current

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the inward Ca2+ current and outward K+ current are roughly equal, holding the potential near 0 mV.
distractorRationale.b: Fast Na+ channels inactivate within milliseconds and do not sustain the plateau.
distractorRationale.c: Ca2+ enters the cell during phase 2; K+ leaves.
distractorRationale.d: If all channels closed, the membrane potential would not be held at a depolarised level.

questions.explanation: During phase 2, L-type Ca2+ channels carry inward current that is opposed by outward K+ current through delayed-rectifier channels, so the membrane potential stays near 0 mV for about 200 ms. The Ca2+ entering also triggers contraction.

questions.stem: Which description best explains the spontaneous diastolic depolarisation of sinoatrial node cells?

options.text: A slow inward funny current through HCN channels with declining K+ efflux, then T-type Ca2+ entry, brings the membrane to threshold
Stable open inward rectifier K+ channels keep the cell at -90 mV until a stimulus arrives from the atrium
Fast Na+ channels open spontaneously at rest to depolarise the cell
A rise in extracellular Ca2+ opens the plateau currents

questions.correctOptionText: A slow inward funny current through HCN channels with declining K+ efflux, then T-type Ca2+ entry, brings the membrane to threshold

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the pacemaker potential is built from If, falling K+ current and T-type Ca2+ current.
distractorRationale.b: Stable IK1 describes ventricular and atrial myocytes, not SA node cells which lack a stable resting potential.
distractorRationale.c: Nodal cells have few fast Na+ channels and the upstroke is carried by Ca2+.
distractorRationale.d: The plateau is a feature of ventricular cells and is not the pacemaker mechanism.

questions.explanation: SA node cells have no stable resting potential. The funny current through HCN channels, a falling outward K+ current and then T-type Ca2+ entry produce a slow phase 4 depolarisation that reaches threshold, at which L-type Ca2+ channels generate the upstroke.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with heart failure taking a potassium-sparing diuretic and an ACE inhibitor has a plasma potassium that remains markedly raised for several hours. Which mechanism best explains the reduced excitability of her ventricular myocytes?

options.text: Sustained depolarisation inactivates fast Na+ channels, so fewer are available to open
The resting potential becomes more negative, moving it away from threshold
L-type Ca2+ channels permanently open, leaving the cell unable to repolarise
The Na+ concentration gradient across the membrane collapses

questions.correctOptionText: Sustained depolarisation inactivates fast Na+ channels, so fewer are available to open

distractorRationale.a: Correct: persistent depolarisation keeps Na+ channels inactivated, lowering upstroke velocity, excitability and conduction.
distractorRationale.b: Raising extracellular K+ makes EK less negative, so the resting potential becomes less negative, not more negative.
distractorRationale.c: L-type Ca2+ channels do not become permanently open in hyperkalaemia.
distractorRationale.d: The Na+ gradient is not collapsed; the Na+ channel state is what changes.

questions.explanation: A higher extracellular K+ shifts EK and the resting potential to less negative values. If this depolarisation persists, fast Na+ channels stay inactivated, which slows the upstroke and conduction and reduces excitability, risking block or arrhythmia.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sinoatrial node, the upstroke of the action potential (phase 0) is carried mainly by fast voltage-gated Na+ channels.
questions.explanation: Nodal cells have few fast Na+ channels, and at their less negative maximum diastolic potential most are inactivated. The upstroke is carried by L-type Ca2+ channels, which is why it is slower than in ventricular myocytes.

questions.stem: A patient after a crush injury has plasma [K+] of 6.0 mmol/L, while intracellular [K+] is 140 mmol/L. Using EK = 61.5 x log10([K+]o / [K+]i) mV, calculate the potassium equilibrium potential in mV.
questions.explanation: The ratio is 6 / 140 = 0.0429 and log10(0.0429) = -1.368. Multiplying by 61.5 mV gives EK = -84 mV. Compared with about -95 mV at normal [K+] of 4 mmol/L, this is about 11 mV less negative, so the resting potential moves towards threshold and sodium channels begin to be inactivated.

questions.stem: Extracellular [K+] doubles from 4 to 8 mmol/L while intracellular [K+] stays constant. Using EK = 61.5 x log10([K+]o / [K+]i) mV, by how many mV does EK become less negative (give the magnitude of the shift)?
questions.explanation: Because [K+]i is constant, the shift equals 61.5 x log10(8 / 4) = 61.5 x log10(2) = 61.5 x 0.301 = 18.5 mV. A doubling of external K+ therefore depolarises EK by about 18.5 mV regardless of the starting values, which is almost as large as the roughly 20 to 25 mV gap between the resting potential and threshold of a ventricular myocyte.

questions.stem: Describe the five phases of the ventricular myocyte action potential, naming the main ion movement in each phase, and state why the long plateau is physiologically important.
markingGuide: Phase 4: resting potential about -90 mV maintained by K+ efflux through inward rectifier channels (IK1)
Phase 0: rapid depolarisation by influx of Na+ through fast voltage-gated channels
Phase 1: early repolarisation as Na+ channels inactivate and transient outward K+ current flows
Phase 2: plateau from inward Ca2+ through L-type channels balanced by outward K+
Phase 3: repolarisation as Ca2+ channels close and delayed-rectifier K+ efflux dominates
Plateau prolongs the refractory period, preventing tetanus and allowing ventricular filling; Ca2+ entry supports contraction
questions.explanation: The five phases are 4 (resting), 0 (Na+ influx), 1 (early repolarisation), 2 (Ca2+ influx balanced by K+ efflux) and 3 (K+ efflux). The plateau lengthens the refractory period to nearly the duration of the contraction, so the ventricle cannot be tetanised and has time to relax and fill.

questions.stem: Explain how sinoatrial node cells generate spontaneous depolarisation and why the SA node, rather than other cardiac tissue, sets the heart rate.
markingGuide: SA node cells have no stable resting potential; maximum diastolic potential about -60 mV
Phase 4 pacemaker potential from the funny current (HCN channels, inward Na+) activated on repolarisation
Falling outward K+ current contributes, and T-type Ca2+ current late in phase 4
At threshold (about -40 mV) L-type Ca2+ channels open, producing the upstroke; K+ efflux repolarises
SA node has the fastest rate of spontaneous depolarisation, so it reaches threshold first and drives other tissue
questions.explanation: In phase 4 the funny current, a declining K+ efflux and T-type Ca2+ entry slowly depolarise SA node cells from about -60 mV to threshold, where L-type Ca2+ channels generate the upstroke. Because the SA node depolarises faster than any other cardiac tissue, it reaches threshold first and sets the heart rate.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with a prolonged crush injury and acute kidney injury has a plasma potassium of 7.2 mmol/L. Predict the effect on the resting membrane potential and excitability of ventricular myocytes, explaining each step, and state the clinical consequence.
markingGuide: Raised extracellular K+ reduces the K+ gradient, so EK (Nernst) becomes less negative
Resting potential is determined mainly by K+ permeability, so the cell is depolarised
Initially the cell is closer to threshold, so excitability may be transiently increased
Sustained depolarisation inactivates fast Na+ channels, reducing upstroke velocity, conduction velocity and excitability
Raised K+ increases K+ conductance and shortens the action potential (faster repolarisation)
Consequences: slowed or blocked conduction and risk of arrhythmias including ventricular fibrillation or asystole
questions.explanation: A rise in extracellular K+ makes EK less negative, depolarising the resting potential. If depolarisation persists, fast Na+ channels become inactivated, so the upstroke is slower, conduction is slowed and excitability falls. The shortened action potential and slow conduction predispose to conduction block and fatal arrhythmias.
